# The Peculiar Comfort of Incomplete Things

I've been thinking lately about unfinished sentences, abandoned projects, and the strange peace they can bring. There's something liberating about incompleteness that our culture rarely celebrates. We're obsessed with closure, with finished products, with the satisfying click of a solved puzzle. But some of my favorite possessions are things that will never be complete, and some of my best thoughts happen in the spaces between ideas.

My grandmother left behind a quilt she never finished. It's draped across my guest room chair—maybe thirty percent done at most. The backing is pinned to the frame, patches of fabric are sewn together in one corner, and threads dangle from places where stitching began but stopped. For years I thought about finishing it myself, but I've come to treasure it exactly as it is. It's become a meditation on intention and mortality. She chose that fabric, threaded that needle, sat with that quilt in her lap during afternoons I'll never know about. The unfinished state somehow preserves her presence more completely than a done quilt ever could. Completion would have felt like erasing her.

There's a park near my house with a walking trail that I've never finished. Every time I walk it, I turn back at a different point. I've never reached the end. I like it this way. It means there's always more to discover, always a "next time" that might reveal something new. The trees are different in each season, the light angles differently depending on the hour, and I've met different people at different turning-around points. By never finishing the trail, I've somehow experienced it more thoroughly than someone who hiked to the end once and never returned.

I think about how books end, too—or rather, how they seem to end, how ending is almost always a kind of violence against a story. The characters didn't really stop existing, they didn't really resolve all their complications. We just stopped reading. The most real characters in literature are the ones who feel like they're continuing on without us, who seem like they have thoughts and struggles we'll never know about. The incompleteness of our knowledge about them is what makes them feel alive.

This connects to something I've noticed about conversations. The best conversations are the ones that feel incomplete when they end—when you both have to leave but could have talked for hours, when there's still something hanging in the air. It's different from an unsatisfying conversation that fizzles out. This is more like a conversation that has momentum, that leaves both people thinking about what might have been said next, feeling the gap between what was expressed and what remained unsaid.

Modern productivity culture wants us to believe that everything should be done, shipped, finished, checked off. But this creates a peculiar anxiety. Once something is finished, it's vulnerable to judgment. It's vulnerable to being wrong. An unfinished project lives in a state of potential—it could be anything, it could be brilliant, it could be exactly what the world needs. The moment you declare it finished, you're claiming something definite about it.

I have notebooks filled with half-finished essays, abandoned stories, fragments of ideas that didn't cohere. There's something I wrote once about the color blue that's only three paragraphs. I didn't finish it because I said everything I needed to say, and continuing felt like lying. It sits there in its incompleteness, and occasionally I'll flip to it and think about what else might be true about blue, but I don't write it. The three paragraphs contain exactly the moment of understanding that was real.

There's a musical phrase I play on my old guitar sometimes—maybe eight or ten notes. It's not part of a song I'm learning. It's just something I started playing one evening and it felt good so I kept it. I've never finished turning it into anything. I'll never play a complete song with a beginning, middle, and end. But playing those notes is more satisfying to me than playing through an entire piece of classical music would be. It's my own little loop of incompleteness.

I wonder if this is what meditation is actually about—learning to sit with something incomplete, with a thought that doesn't resolve, with a breath that will soon become another breath, with a moment that yields to the next moment without climax or closure.

The danger of embracing incompleteness, of course, is that it can become an excuse for avoidance. There's a difference between a genuinely unfinished thing and a thing you're afraid to finish. The quilt my grandmother never finished was a true incompletion—she ran out of time. My three paragraphs about blue are genuinely complete as a thought, even if they're incomplete as a piece of writing. But a project abandoned out of fear, or perfectionism, or depression—that's something else. That's not the beauty of incompletion; that's the ugliness of paralysis.

Yet even with that caveat, I think we could all stand to be a little more comfortable with incompleteness. To leave some corners of our lives unfinished. To have thoughts that don't resolve into a neat conclusion. To work on things we'll probably never finish. To read a poem multiple times without ever feeling like we've completely understood it. To love people and know there will always be more to discover about them.

The nineteenth-century Japanese artists and poets embraced a concept called *wabi-sabi*—finding beauty in incompleteness, impermanence, and imperfection. A tea bowl with an asymmetrical shape, a garden with empty space, a poem that ends with a gesture toward something unsaid. This wasn't a consolation prize for the inability to achieve perfection. It was a recognition that perfection, completion, and symmetry might actually be less beautiful than their opposites.

I'm going to leave this essay unfinished, too. Not because I've run out of words or ideas—I could probably keep going—but because there's something right about stopping here, in this space where you might be wondering what comes next, where the thread of the thought continues somewhere I'm not going to articulate. You'll finish the thought yourself. You'll add your own incomplete memories, your own unfinished projects. And that incompleteness, that gap between what I've said and what I meant, between what you've read and what you're imagining—that's where something real happens.
